name: Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-3
lead: Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-3 is a cosmetic ingredient classed among the signal peptides, short amino-acid chains attached to a fatty (palmitoyl) group and added to skin-care products. It appears by name in the ingredient lists of published patent compositions for topical products, where it is combined with plant extracts and other actives [1][2][3].

Published scientific literature on this specific ingredient is sparse in the sources reviewed for this wiki. No clinical trial of palmitoyl tetrapeptide-3 was found, and the available records only show it as one listed component of multi-ingredient formulations, so its effect on appearance has not been established by independent human studies.
infobox: Ingredient in multi-component serums and creams
Cosmetic ingredient; no drug approval found

paras: A family of patent filings from 2008 to 2010 describes compositions containing at least two of a long list of ingredients, among them magnolia extract, honokiol, hesperidin methyl chalcone, gotu kola, a valine-tryptophan dipeptide, ascorbyl glucoside and palmitoyl tetrapeptide-3 [1][2][3]. These filings illustrate how the peptide is used as one ingredient among many rather than as a stand-alone product.

A related, better-documented cosmetic peptide, palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (sold as Matrixyl), was launched by the manufacturer Sederma in 2000 and is promoted for anti-wrinkle use; it is a different molecule from palmitoyl tetrapeptide-3 [4].
No studies found. The only records located are patent filings that list the peptide as an ingredient; they do not report human trial results [1][2][3].

card.summary: A cosmetic signal peptide that shows up in serum ingredient lists, with no published human trials behind it.
card.note: Known only as one ingredient in multi-ingredient formulations; no clinical studies found.

quick.overview:
Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-3 is a short peptide linked to a fatty chain, used as an ingredient in some skin-care products. It is grouped with other cosmetic signal peptides.

It is documented mainly in patent filings that list it among many ingredients. No human trials of the ingredient itself were found.
quick.mechanism: Signal peptides are generally described by manufacturers as messengers that prompt skin cells; the sources reviewed here do not describe a tested mechanism for this specific peptide.
quick.risks: No safety data specific to this ingredient were found. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient rather than as an approved drug.
